readingInstruction: Read Hebrews 11:1-40. This chapter is often called the “hall of faith,” and it is worth reading it as a story rather than a list. Notice how each person acts on a promise they cannot yet see. As you read, pay attention to how the chapter begins with a definition and ends with a surprise: none of them received what was promised.
settingTheScene: The last chapter ended with a call to endurance: “the righteous shall live by faith.” Chapter 11 is the author’s answer to the question, what does that look like? He walks through the Old Testament, and the people you have been reading about in this plan appear one after another: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Rahab, and many more. Their stories are different, but their faith has the same shape. They believed God’s word about what he would do, and they lived accordingly. For readers who were tired and tempted to quit, this was a gallery of encouragement. For us, it is a review of much of the Old Testament through the lens of faith.
observation: “Faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (11:1).
“By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God” (11:3).
Abel, Enoch, and Noah are praised for worship, walking with God, and obedience on the basis of a warning about what was not yet seen (11:4-7).
Abraham went out “not knowing where he was going” and lived as a sojourner in tents (11:8-10).
These all “died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar” (11:13).
They desired “a better country, that is, a heavenly one,” and God “has prepared for them a city” (11:16).
Verses 32-38 list others whose faith led to victory and others whose faith led to suffering, torture, and exile.
“God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect” (11:40).
interpretation:
The chapter begins with a definition. Faith is the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen. It is not a leap in the dark or wishful thinking. It is confidence in what God has said, which stands on his character and promise. Faith gives substance to what is hoped for and evidence for what cannot yet be seen.

The author illustrates this with an extended survey. Some things stand out. First, faith always responds to a word. Noah heard a warning. Abraham heard a call. Moses heard a promise. Faith is not generated from within. It is a response to God speaking. Second, faith acts. Abel offered. Noah built. Abraham went. Sarah considered him faithful who had promised. Faith is not merely inward conviction. It is obedience.

Third, faith endures. Notice verses 13-16. These people lived as strangers and exiles on the earth. They could have returned to the land they left, but they desired a better country. Because of that, “God is not ashamed to be called their God.” Faith is not fully satisfied by this world. It looks for a city with foundations, whose designer and builder is God.

The most remarkable examples come in verses 17-19. Abraham, when tested, offered up Isaac, “considering that God was able even to raise him from the dead.” You read this in Genesis 22. The author reveals what was going on in Abraham’s mind: he believed in resurrection before it happened. That is the kind of faith that makes sense of an impossible command.

Verses 32-38 are striking. The author, running short of time, summarizes: some by faith conquered kingdoms, shut the mouths of lions, and escaped the edge of the sword. Others by faith were tortured, mocked, imprisoned, and killed. “Of whom the world was not worthy.” Both groups are commended for faith. Faith is not a guarantee of success or comfort. Sometimes it leads to victory in this life, and sometimes to suffering. In either case, God honors it.

Then comes the surprise. “And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us.” The Old Testament saints waited, and we are living in the fulfillment of what they longed for. Christ has come. And they will not be made perfect without us. The family of faith is one, and its completion awaits all of God’s people together.

This is the proper way to read the chapter. It does not tell you to be like the heroes. It tells you that God was faithful to them, and that he will be faithful to you. The “cloud of witnesses” in the next chapter will be exactly these people, and they are cheering for you to run the race that they have finished.
connection: Nearly every person in this chapter appears in the Old Testament stories you have read in this plan: Genesis 4 (Abel), Genesis 5 (Enoch), Genesis 6-9 (Noah), Genesis 12-22 (Abraham and Sarah), Genesis 27-50 (Isaac, Jacob, Joseph), and Exodus (Moses). The definition of faith recalls Genesis 15:6. The better country anticipates Revelation 21-22. The unnamed sufferers of verses 35-38 recall the prophets and the Maccabean martyrs, and the idea of God’s people waiting for the whole body to be completed anticipates Revelation 6:9-11.
application:
First, think about how you define faith. If you think of it as a feeling or a general positive attitude, let this chapter correct you. Faith is trusting what God has said and acting on it.

Second, identify one area where God has given you a clear word, in Scripture, but you have not yet acted. It might be forgiving someone, giving generously, or sharing the gospel. Take one concrete step.

Third, be encouraged that faith does not always bring ease. If you are suffering and wondering whether you are doing something wrong, notice the second half of the list. Faithful people suffered too. God was not ashamed of them.

Fourth, look at the “better” in verse 40. We have received what they longed for. Thank God that you live on this side of the cross.
prayerPrompts: Ask God for faith that trusts his word when you cannot see the outcome.
Name a person from the chapter whose faith you want to follow.
Thank him that they all point to Jesus.
